hints: Recall the definition of isotopes in terms of proton number $Z$ and neutron number $N$ for the same element.
teacher_walkthrough: Isotopes of the same element are defined by equal proton number $Z$ and different neutron number $N$.
Nuclear charge is determined only by protons as $$Q = Ze$$ where $e$ is the elementary charge.
Since $Z_X = Z_Y$, then $Q_X = Z_X e = Z_Y e = Q_Y$, so the charge of X is the same as the charge of Y.
walkthrough: X and Y are isotopes so have same number of protons.
Charge depends on proton number, so charge of X is the same as charge of Y.
common_pitfalls: Stating that different isotopes have different proton numbers; isotopes differ only in neutrons.
Thinking that extra neutrons change nuclear charge; neutrons are neutral and do not affect $Q = Ze$.

hints: Recall what happens to a proton in $\beta^{+}$ decay and how proton number $Z$ changes.
Link the change in proton number to nuclear charge using $Q = Ze$ to compare X and Z.
teacher_walkthrough: $\beta^{+}$ decay is the conversion of a proton to a neutron in the nucleus: $$p \rightarrow n + \beta^{+} + \nu_{e}$$
Proton number decreases by one, so if X decays to Z then $$Z_Z = Z_X - 1$$ which rearranges to $$Z_X = Z_Z + 1$$
Nuclear charge is $$Q = Ze$$ so $$Q_X = Z_X e$$ is larger than $$Q_Z = Z_Z e$$ by one elementary charge, therefore charge of X is greater than charge of Z.
walkthrough: In $\beta^{+}$ emission X has one more proton than Z.
Greater proton number means greater positive charge, so X has greater charge than Z.
common_pitfalls: Reversing the $Z$ change and stating $Z$ increases in $\beta^{+}$ decay; $\beta^{-}$ increases $Z$ while $\beta^{+}$ decreases $Z$.
Comparing nucleon number $A$ instead of proton number $Z$; $A$ is unchanged in beta decay but charge follows $Z$.

hints: Recall the two classes of hadrons that experience the strong interaction: baryons and the other group.
teacher_walkthrough: Hadrons are particles that interact via the strong nuclear force.
Hadrons are divided into two classes: baryons and mesons.
Since group P is baryons, group Q must be mesons.
walkthrough: The other hadron group besides baryons is mesons.
common_pitfalls: Answering leptons or quarks; leptons are not hadrons and quarks are constituents, not hadron classes.
Confusing mesons with muons; muons are leptons with similar symbol $\mu$ but unrelated to hadrons.

hints: Contrast with baryons which contain three quarks, and recall the quark plus antiquark combination for the other hadron class.
teacher_walkthrough: Quark model for hadrons: baryons consist of three quarks $(qqq)$.
Mesons are the other hadron class and consist of one quark and one antiquark $(q\bar{q})$.
Therefore hadrons in group Q each contain a $q\bar{q}$ pair.
walkthrough: Mesons consist of one quark and one antiquark.
common_pitfalls: Stating three quarks or three antiquarks; that structure describes baryons and antibaryons, not mesons.
Stating a single quark; a single isolated quark is not a hadron due to confinement, hadrons must be $qqq$ or $q\bar{q}$.
